page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The statement
lines: The rule applies when an unsymmetrical
reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene.
The negative part of the reagent adds to
The positive part adds to the other
carbon, the one with more hydrogen atoms.
steps.why: Both carbons of a double bond can take the incoming halogen, so a rule is needed to say which of the two products actually forms. The number of hydrogen atoms on each carbon decides it, and that is a thing a student can read straight off the structure.
common_mistakes: Putting the negative part on the carbon with more hydrogen atoms. It goes to the carbon with fewer.
Stating the rule for the positive part only. Name where the negative part goes.
Leaving out the word unsymmetrical. The rule is needed only when both the alkene and the reagent are unsymmetrical.
steps.memory_tip: Fewer hydrogen atoms on the carbon, so that carbon takes the negative part.
steps.margin_note: State the rule for the negative part of the reagent, then give one example.

steps.label: The example
lines: In propene, the end carbon carries two
hydrogen atoms and the middle one carries
Bromine is the negative part, so it adds
steps.why: Propene is the shortest alkene whose two double-bonded carbons differ, so it shows the rule with nothing else in the way: the bromine goes to the carbon with one hydrogen atom and the added hydrogen goes to the carbon with two.
common_mistakes: Writing 1-bromopropane. That is the product the rule rules out for this addition.
Applying the rule to a symmetrical alkene such as ethylene. Both carbons there are alike, so one product is possible anyway.
steps.memory_tip: Bromine adds to the middle carbon of propene, giving 2-bromopropane.
steps.margin_note: Show which carbon carries how many hydrogen atoms before naming the product.
